name: Kedarnath Temple
summary: One of the twelve Jyotirlingas, set in the Garhwal Himalaya — among the most revered and demanding pilgrimages in North India.
mythology: Kedarnath is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas — foremost seats where Shiva is worshipped as a pillar of light (jyoti). In the Mahabharata–linked Garhwal tradition, the Pandavas sought Shiva after the Kurukshetra war. Shiva, avoiding them in the form of a bull, submerged into the earth; the hump remaining at Kedarnath became the object of worship. The Skanda Purana and later Himalayan mahatmya literature celebrate this landscape as part of Shiva’s Himalayan presence.
scriptureLinks: Accounts summarised from widely cited Puranic, epic, and pilgrimage traditions; local tellings may differ.
festivals: Temple opening (Akshaya Tritiya period — dates vary yearly)
Closing before heavy winter (typically Bhai Dooj / Kartik)
Maha Shivaratri (celebrated at Ukhimath winter seat when temple is closed)
bestTime: May–June and September–early October. Monsoon (July–August) brings landslide risk; winter access is closed.
whatToCarry: Warm layers even in summer, rain shell, sturdy trekking shoes, torch, basic medicines, cash, photocopies of ID. Oxygen / pony / helicopter options exist for those who need them — plan ahead.
climate: Alpine. Days can be bright and cold; nights near freezing even in season. Weather changes quickly.
nearestRail: Rishikesh (~210 km) or Haridwar; then road to Gaurikund and trek (~16 km) or helicopter (seasonal).
nearestAirport: Dehradun (Jolly Grant); helicopters operate seasonally from Phata / Guptkashi area subject to weather.
accommodation: GMVN and private lodges in Gaurikund, Guptkashi, Sitapur; limited rooms near temple in season. Book early for peak months. Temple-committee / trust arrangements change yearly — check official yatra portals.
localFood: Simple Garhwali vegetarian thalis, tea stalls, prasadam lines. Pure veg culture dominates the yatra route.
otherFood: Limited non-local options; carry dry snacks/electrolytes for the trek.
localLanguage: Hindi and Garhwali; English understood at major tourist points.
dressCode: Modest clothing covering shoulders and knees. Warm layers essential. No strict dhoti mandate, but remove footwear at the temple.
darshanTimings: Seasonal; typically early morning to evening with short midday breaks. Exact aarti and darshan slots are published each season by the temple administration.
specialEntry: Helicopter tickets and VIP/priority arrangements (when available) are managed through official Uttarakhand yatra / temple portals — avoid unofficial agents.
restrictions: Drones restricted. Plastic rules apply on trek routes. Follow local administration advisories after rain. Leather items: follow queue instructions at entry.
lockers: Limited cloak / luggage facilities at Gaurikund and near temple approaches — confirm on site; travel light for the trek.

mythologySignificance:
Kedarnath is counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas — foremost seats where Shiva is worshipped as a pillar of light (jyoti). In the Mahabharata–linked Garhwal tradition, the Pandavas sought Shiva after the Kurukshetra war. Shiva, avoiding them in the form of a bull, submerged into the earth; the hump remaining at Kedarnath became the object of worship. The Skanda Purana and later Himalayan mahatmya literature celebrate this landscape as part of Shiva’s Himalayan presence.

Kedarnath also belongs to the Uttarakhand Chota Char Dham and to the Panch Kedar set. It is not one of Adi Shankaracharya’s four pan-India Char Dham seats (Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri, Rameswaram).
localBeliefs:
Garhwal pilgrims regard the rocky shrine and surrounding peaks as living presence of Shiva. Adi Shankaracharya is traditionally linked with the temple’s living monastic framework and a samadhi site nearby. In winter, when snow closes the high shrine, worship continues at Ukhimath — a seasonal belief that the deity ‘moves’ with the community.

Many devotees treat the trek itself as tapasya. Local lore also connects nearby Panch Kedar temples to different parts of Shiva’s bull-form.
mythologyDisclaimer: Mythological accounts and local beliefs are drawn from Puranic traditions, epics, and widely recorded sthala-purana / pilgrimage lore. Versions differ by scripture, region, and temple tradition. This section is for cultural understanding — not a claim of historical fact, nor a substitute for guidance from temple priests or official trusts.
